analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $15 for employees of companies with $1 billion-plus annual revenue.
analysis.headline: No other senator signed on and the Senate committee took no action, so the bill died without a vote when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act so that employers with at least $1 billion in annual revenue must pay a rising minimum wage: $9.50 an hour starting three months after enactment, then $11, $12.50, $14, and $15 over four more years. After five years, the wage would rise each year with the growth in the median hourly wage nationwide, as measured by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Tipped employees would be excluded, keeping the existing tip-credit wage for them. The bill went nowhere: it was referred to the Senate committee handling labor matters and never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at large corporations — big-box retailers, fast-food chains, large logistics and other billion-dollar-revenue employers — who earn less than $15 an hour. Under the bill they would see their wage rise from the federal floor of $7.25 to $9.50 within months, then step up to $15 over five years, with future increases tied to median wage growth.

how_it_helps.text: Requires employers with at least $1 billion in annual revenue to pay a minimum wage of $9.50 an hour starting three months after enactment, stepping up to $11, $12.50, $14, and $15 over the following four years.

After five years, the minimum wage for these employers would rise annually by the percentage increase in the median hourly wage of all U.S. employees, as determined by the Secretary of Labor through the Bureau of Labor Statistics, and could never decrease.
The $1 billion revenue threshold targets the raise at the largest employers, leaving businesses under that revenue level out of the mandate entirely.
The requirement would not apply to tipped employees, so the existing lower wage for tipped workers at these employers would continue.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with $1 billion or more in annual revenue would bear higher payroll costs as wages step up to $15, and some of that cost could be passed to consumers through prices or offset through reduced hiring, automation, or restructuring at the margin.

drawbacks.text: Tipped employees are entirely excluded, so restaurant and similar workers at even the largest employers would not get the raise and would remain under the tip-credit wage system.

The $1 billion revenue threshold creates a cliff: employers just under it would have a cost advantage over those just over it, which could push firms to restructure, franchise, or split operations to stay below the line — shifting workers out of the bill's coverage.
The bill covers only employees of billion-dollar-revenue employers, leaving minimum-wage workers at the many smaller businesses without any raise.
It drew zero cosponsors from either party, including from the senator's own party, an honest signal that there was no broader coalition in the Senate to enact it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For covered workers the benefit is direct and substantial: a raise from $7.25 to $15 over five years, tied to wage growth afterward. The design flaws are real — tipped workers get nothing, and the revenue threshold creates avoidance incentives at the margin — but the core mechanism is a straightforward, targeted wage mandate. The bill's bigger weakness was political: not a single other senator supported it, so the flaws never even got tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee in March 2021, and the committee never held a hearing or vote on it; it died there when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Josh Hawley introduced S. 555 in the Senate on March 3, 2021.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No cosponsors joined from either party; the cosponsors list shows zero.
After referral, the action history records no further action — no committee markup, no floor vote — through the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large employers with $1 billion-plus in revenue are better off: they never faced the mandated wage increase, so their payroll costs stayed at the existing federal floor of $7.25 an hour. Covered workers earning less than that are worse off, having lost the chance at the raise when the bill died without a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Billion-dollar employers who avoided the raise

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Introduced S. 555 to raise the minimum wage to $15 for billion-dollar-revenue employers, and was its only supporter in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Referred to the committee in March 2021, the bill sat without any hearing, markup, or vote for the rest of the 117th Congress.

against.name: Senate Republicans and Senate Democrats
against.what_they_did: None signed on as cosponsors; no senator from either party backed the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, so no party bloc ever lined up for or against it.

industries.industry: Large retailers, fast-food chains, and other billion-dollar-revenue employers
industries.note: These employers would have faced a mandated wage floor rising from $9.50 to $15 over five years, increasing payroll costs. Because their gain under the outcome is avoiding a raise their workers would have received, their interest ran against the workers' in this bill.

industries.industry: Tipped-service businesses (restaurants and similar) with $1 billion-plus revenue
industries.note: The bill carved tipped employees out entirely, so even covered large employers could keep paying the lower tip-credit wage to tipped staff. Had the bill died or had it passed, tipped workers at large employers would have remained outside any raise.

industries.industry: Businesses under the $1 billion revenue threshold
industries.note: The bill would have imposed no new wage mandate on them while raising their larger competitors' labor costs, giving them a relative cost advantage. The threshold could also encourage firms near the line to restructure to stay under it.
